title: US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF)
summary: This informational document reproduces the US Secure Hash Algorithms from Federal Information Processing Standards, along with SHA-based HMAC and HKDF. It provides reference code so others can implement and test them. These are widely used hash functions for security protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A hash turns any file into a short fingerprint. This gives the recipes and example code for several popular fingerprint machines used across the internet.

questions: what is the difference between sha-256 and sha-512
subtitle: Open-source reference code for the US SHA-2 hash functions, plus SHA-based HMAC and HKDF.

tldr.problem: The US government standardized a family of Secure Hash Algorithms, but the Internet community wanted convenient, freely usable code and a readable description of them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC restates SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (padding, constants and the block-by-block computation), and supplies C code for them, for SHA-based HMAC, and for the HKDF key derivation function.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that replaces RFC 4634. The authors make no independent claim about the security of the functions.

today: RFC 6234 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4634 and updates RFC 3174. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Document Provides
sections.content:
The United States adopted a suite of Secure Hash Algorithms in a Federal Information Processing Standard: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (SHA-1 is specified separately in RFC 3174). RFC 6234 makes open source code for them available to the Internet community, and the sample code accepts input strings of any bit length. Much of the text is adapted from FIPS 180-2.

Given a message shorter than 2^64 bits (SHA-224 and SHA-256) or 2^128 bits (SHA-384 and SHA-512), each function outputs a message digest between 224 and 512 bits long. The RFC calls them secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message for a given digest, or two different messages with the same digest.

The document also includes code for HMAC and for HKDF, but the specifications of those two live in RFC 2104 and RFC 5869.

The assertions about the security of the algorithms are made by the US Government, the author of the standard, not by the authors of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a cookbook plus ready-made kitchen tools for making short fingerprints of any message, so everyone can make the same fingerprint the same way.

sections.title: Notation and Word Operations
sections.content:
The algorithms work on words: 32-bit words for SHA-224 and SHA-256, and 64-bit words for SHA-384 and SHA-512. A word is written as 8 or 16 hex digits, and the RFC uses the big-endian convention, so the most significant bit is on the left. A block is a 512-bit or 1024-bit string.

The building blocks are bitwise AND, OR, XOR and NOT, addition modulo 2^w, a right shift SHR, and a rotate right ROTR (with ROTL as its mirror image). All addition inside the algorithms is done modulo 2^32 or 2^64.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe only uses simple moves, like shuffling and mixing bits, the way you might shuffle a deck of cards over and over.

sections.title: Message Padding and Parsing
sections.content:
Before hashing, the message is padded so its length is a multiple of the block size. The rule is the same for every algorithm: append a 1 bit, then K zero bits, then the original length L as a 64-bit integer (SHA-224 and SHA-256) or a 128-bit integer (SHA-384 and SHA-512).

K is the smallest non-negative solution of (L + 1 + K) mod 512 = 448 for SHA-224 and SHA-256, or (L + 1 + K) mod 1024 = 896 for SHA-384 and SHA-512. The RFC works an example with the five bytes abcde: L is 40, so 407 zero bits are added for SHA-256 and 855 for SHA-512, and the length field reads 28 in hex.

The padded message is then split into 512-bit or 1024-bit blocks that are processed one after another.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine packing items into boxes of one exact size. You fill the leftover space with filler and write on the box how much real stuff is inside.

sections.title: Computing the Digest
sections.content:
Each algorithm keeps a hash value of eight words, starting from fixed initial values. SHA-256 and SHA-512 take theirs from the fractional parts of square roots of prime numbers. SHA-224 and SHA-384 use different initial values and produce a shorter output by leaving out some of the final words.

For every block the algorithm builds a message schedule: the 16 words of the block are expanded to 64 words (SHA-224 and SHA-256) or 80 words (SHA-384 and SHA-512). Eight working variables a to h are then updated once per schedule word, using the functions CH, MAJ, BSIG0, BSIG1, SSIG0 and SSIG1 and a table of constants derived from cube roots of primes. The results are added to the running hash value.

SHA-224 and SHA-256 differ only in their starting values and in how the final output is formed. The same is true of SHA-384 and SHA-512.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box gets stirred into a big pot using the same fixed steps. After the last box, what is left in the pot is the fingerprint.

sections.title: HMAC, HKDF and the C Code
sections.content:
HMAC (RFC 2104) mixes a secret key into a hash to produce a keyed authentication code. HKDF (RFC 5869) is an HMAC-based function that turns initial keying material into one or more strong secret keys. Both were devised by Hugo Krawczyk. This RFC does not respecify them; it gives sample code.

The bulk of the document is a demonstration implementation in C: header files, sha1.c, sha224-256.c, sha384-512.c, usha.c, the HMAC and HKDF code, and a test driver. Defining USE_32BIT_ONLY at compile time avoids 64-bit operations. The HMAC code accepts input of any number of octets and bits and also offers a fixed-length interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the fingerprint recipe, the document includes working tools, written in a programming language, so people can check their own tools give the same answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Changes
sections.content:
The document aims to give convenient open source access to the FIPS Secure Hash Algorithms, to HMACs based on them, and to HKDF. It states that no independent assertion of security by the authors is intended, and points to RFC 6194 for the security considerations of SHA-1.

Compared with RFC 4634, this version adds HKDF and fixes errata. The earlier code never returned an incorrect hash value, but some error codes were wrong, and the SHA-384 and SHA-512 code used to stop after 2^93 bytes. The fixed code handles up to 2^125 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say they are sharing the recipe and tools, but they are not promising on their own that the recipe is unbreakable.
